analysis.one_liner: Applies federal-agency-style privacy rules to internet companies' handling of users' personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its Senate committee referral: it received no committee action and no floor vote, and drew zero cosponsors before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring internet companies to follow privacy practices similar to those that bind federal agencies under the Privacy Act of 1974. Companies would have to restrict who they share user records with, let people see and correct their own records, keep an accounting of disclosures, and follow a code of fair information practices. Small startups could be exempted, and the bill would have preempted state privacy laws for covered companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users. They would gain a legal right to access and correct the personal records companies keep on them, restrictions on how companies sell or disclose those records, and a no-cost dispute process for inaccurate data — the same basic rights federal employees have over their own agency files.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users whose data is tracked

how_it_helps.text: Gives individuals the right to request access to records a company maintains about them, with the company required to provide access or delete the record on request.
Requires companies to amend records shown to be inaccurate, irrelevant, untimely, or incomplete, through a dispute process modeled on the Fair Credit Reporting Act that costs the individual nothing.
Restricts disclosure of user records and requires companies to keep an accounting of certain disclosures, available to the individual on request.
Exempts certain small and newly formed providers, based on operating time, revenue, and number of individuals tracked, so the rules concentrate on large data holders.

analysis.who_pays: Internet companies and the businesses built on collecting and reselling personal data, which would face new compliance duties and limits on how they monetize user records. Consumers could also face some indirect costs if companies pass compliance expenses along.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have superseded state privacy laws covering the same records, potentially capping stronger protections in states with stricter rules than the FTC's federal standard.

Enforcement would rest entirely with the FTC under the Federal Trade Commission Act; there is no private right of action for individuals, so protection depends on the commission's priorities and resources.
Companies already covered by HIPAA, FERPA, or the Privacy Act would be exempt for that data, leaving gaps depending on which regime applies to which information.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: today, people generally have no legal right to see or correct the profiles companies keep on them, and this bill would create one. The design has genuine weaknesses — federal preemption could block states from going further, enforcement depends on a single agency, and sectoral exemptions leave holes — so it is a meaningful but imperfect floor rather than the strongest possible privacy law.

outcome.mechanism: Rubio introduced it in January 2019 and it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Marco Rubio introduced the bill on January 16, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was taken in the Senate before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
No senators joined as cosponsors during the two-year window.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Internet platforms, data brokers, and advertisers that collect and sell personal information are better off: the privacy obligations the bill would have imposed never took effect, and no comparable federal law replaced it during the Congress.

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and submitted it to the Senate; no senator cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in January 2019 and took no action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Roger Wicker
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: As committee chair through the 116th Congress, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and no cosponsor signed on, so the bill never revealed whether support or opposition split by party; it was a single Republican sponsor acting alone.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed Privacy Act-style duties on any internet service that collects user records, cutting into the data-collection business model; at the same time, its preemption of state law would have capped stricter state rules like California's, which platforms favor.

These businesses profit from buying, selling, and disclosing personal records; the bill's disclosure restrictions, accounting requirements, and access-and-correction rights would directly constrain that trade.
The FTC was directed to exempt small, newly formed providers based on age, revenue, and number of users tracked, sparing the smallest firms the compliance burden their larger competitors would face.
